bull_thesis:
Encompass Health is the largest operator of inpatient rehabilitation hospitals in the United States, and the bull case is that the market is paying a mediocre-operator multiple for a business that is quietly compounding at high and rising rates of return. Start with the supply-demand arithmetic, which is the closest thing to a structural certainty in this file. The population aged 75 and over is growing about 4% a year, the average patient here is 77 to 78 years old, and management notes that the supply of licensed inpatient rehabilitation beds 'has increased only nominally' because new hospitals require both a state certificate-of-need approval in many markets and compliance with a federal rule limiting which patients qualify. Demand rises against a nearly fixed supply. The company is the only participant meaningfully adding to that supply: 517 beds in 2025, roughly 540 to 590 planned for 2026, and a disclosed pipeline of new hospitals beyond that, now joined by a third format - small satellite hospitals that operate under an existing hospital's Medicare licence and therefore extend the network into markets too small for a full build.

Second, the operating record is exceptional and it checks out against the numbers rather than merely against the narrative. Revenue grew 10.5% in 2025 and adjusted operating profit grew 14.9%, so the operating leverage management claims is real. Free cash flow reached $818 million in 2025, up 18.5%, comfortably funding $736 million of capital spending, $158 million of buybacks and $71 million of dividends while long-term debt stayed essentially flat and net leverage fell from 2.2 times to 1.9 times. The hardest problem in this industry is labor, and it is being solved visibly: nurse turnover fell from 20.4% to 17.8%, the lowest since at least 2012, and premium labor spending fell in five consecutive quarters and by more than $21 million across 2025 even as headcount grew with new hospitals. Return on invested capital is roughly 13.3% on a trailing basis and rising, against a mid-single-digit cost of capital.

Third, and least appreciated, the relative-value case is the opposite of what a cash-flow screen suggests. On enterprise value to operating profit before depreciation - the multiple that is not distorted by growth spending - Encompass Health trades at about 9.6 times trailing and about 9.0 times on 2026 guidance. Select Medical, the closest post-acute comparison, trades at about 9.7 times while earning roughly 4.8% on invested capital with 5.7 times leverage. Ensign Group, the other post-acute operator the market treats as a compounder, trades at about 18.9 times on 7.1% returns. Encompass earns nearly three times Select Medical's returns on a third of the leverage and pays the same multiple. The apparent expensiveness on a price-to-free-cash-flow basis is an accounting consequence of choosing to spend about 12% of revenue on capital projects at more than twice the depreciation rate; strip the growth spending out and maintenance free cash flow is roughly $6.70 a share, a 5.9% yield.

Fourth, management is credible in the specific, testable sense. Guidance has been raised in five consecutive quarters, each time attributed to a quarter already banked; earnings have beaten in seven of seven; and free cash flow guidance was raised three times in 2025 before landing above the top of the final range. They volunteer bad news without being asked - the 85 basis points of discharge drag from deliberate unit closures, the 70 basis point 2026 headwind from the West Virginia closure, the write-off of 2013-vintage claims.

The conditions this case depends on: same-store discharge growth must recover from the 1.6% printed in the first quarter of 2026 back toward 3% or better once the four closed units anniversary, confirming management's account that the deceleration was self-inflicted market consolidation rather than a broken growth algorithm; the pre-payment claim-review programme now live in Texas and California must produce approval rates near the roughly 93% achieved in Alabama; and the annual Medicare rate update must continue to land near the proposed 2.4%.
bear_thesis:
The bear case does not require anything to break. It only requires that a good business already trading at a fair price grows a little more slowly than the market assumes, and it starts with the one number in the file that genuinely deteriorated. Same-store discharge growth ran above 4% for twelve consecutive quarters through 2025 and then printed 1.6% in the first quarter of 2026. Management attributes about 85 basis points to four deliberate unit closures, which still leaves roughly 2.5% underlying - a little more than half the prior run rate. The company's growth formula has been total discharge growth of 6% to 8%, split between new capacity and same-store. If the same-store leg has permanently halved, the whole algorithm resets lower, and at roughly 19 times 2026 adjusted earnings the stock is not priced for that reset.

The regulatory pressure is not theoretical and it is landing now, all at once. Pre-payment claim review expanded into Texas on March 1 and California on May 1 of this year - the two largest states in the network - meaning claims must clear review before payment, which lengthens cash collection and creates denial risk in markets that had none. The bundled-payment pilot that began January 1, 2026 covers 89 Encompass hospitals and pays acute-care hospitals to manage the total cost of an episode, giving the referral source a direct financial reason to route patients to cheaper settings than inpatient rehabilitation. Managed-care friction persists on top of that: management concedes the ratio of admissions to referrals for Medicare Advantage patients is 'substantially below' fee-for-service and that pre-authorization 'is still a grind every day.' Roughly $21 million of 2026 profit comes from state Medicaid provider-tax programmes, exactly the category of regulatory rent current federal policy is aimed at. Management's own words in the first quarter of 2026 were that the company 'will not be immune from short-term transitory impacts.'

The cash math is turning at the wrong moment. First-quarter 2026 adjusted free cash flow fell 12.9% year over year to $193.8 million even as profits grew - the capital programme is now consuming the incremental earnings. Capital spending runs about 12% of revenue at more than twice the depreciation rate, and management has raised that plan four separate times across five calls while explicitly declining to attach a return hurdle to at least one major project. Meanwhile the cost of that capital stepped up: on May 14, 2026 the company priced $500 million of 5.875% notes due 2034 and called $400 million of 4.500% notes due 2028, roughly 140 basis points more expensive, into a rate regime our house work reads as more likely to tighten than ease.

There is also an unresolved reputational and legal overhang that goes to the heart of the pricing model. A July 2025 press investigation, citing federal data, reported that 34 Encompass facilities were rated by Medicare as having statistically significantly worse rates of potentially preventable readmissions; the shares fell 10.35% that day to $107.28. Shareholder legal investigations were opened in March and April 2026 alleging a class period of January 2023 to July 2025. The settlement value of such a case is immaterial against an $11.4 billion company. The real risk is that the same federal readmission data underpins quality-linked reimbursement and could invite a payment-integrity review. Management has answered this question three times about referral patterns and never once about the readmission statistics themselves.

Finally, and decisively for timing: there is no discount here to be paid for taking these risks. The entire hospital sector has de-rated on reimbursement anxiety this year - the large acute-care operators trade roughly 30% to 39% below their own 52-week highs - and Encompass has conspicuously not participated, sitting about 10% off its high and roughly 7% above its 200-day average. Insiders sold 193,117 shares across twelve transactions with zero open-market purchases. The screener's own cash-flow-based valuation methods read deeply negative margins of safety. What confirms the bear: an August 5 report showing same-store discharge growth still near or below 2%, or claim-approval rates in Texas and California materially below the Alabama experience.
consensus_delta:
The usual deep-value question is whether the market is pricing terminal decline into a company with stable or growing earnings power. Here the answer is no, and that is the finding. The market is not pricing decline at all: the consensus target of $146 implies 27% upside, the shares sit about 10% off their 52-week high, and while the acute-care hospital cohort has been savaged this year on reimbursement fear - HCA roughly 30% below its high, Universal Health about 34% below, Community Health about 39% below - Encompass has not participated. The market has already sorted this company out of the distressed group and into the quality group. There is no fear print to buy.

Where we do disagree with the market is narrower and more specific. The published targets are stale relative to the one thing that changed. The newest is 66 days old (Whit Mayo at $152, May 22, 2026, when the stock was $104.45); Barclays at $140 dates from May 5; the $150 marks from UBS and Andrew Mok date from October 2025, when the stock traded around $125. Only two targets printed in the last quarter, so this is not a street-wide view at all - it is two analysts. More to the point, those marks embed the growth algorithm as it stood before same-store discharge growth fell from a twelve-quarter run above 4% to 1.6% in the first quarter of 2026, and before pre-payment claim review went live in California on May 1. The street is still underwriting 6% to 8% total discharge growth split between new capacity and same-store; if the same-store leg has structurally halved rather than temporarily dipped, the algorithm resets and roughly 19 times 2026 adjusted earnings is not a discount to anything.

The second disagreement runs the other way, and it partly offsets the first. Both our own peer file and the broader cash-flow screens call this stock expensive on a 26.3 times price-to-free-cash-flow basis. That reading is wrong, or at least mismeasured. The company deliberately spends about 12% of revenue on capital projects at more than twice its depreciation rate to add 520 to 590 beds a year; free cash flow is suppressed by choice, not by weakness. On enterprise value to operating profit before depreciation it trades at about 9.0 times forward, level with Select Medical, which earns a third of the return on three times the leverage, and at less than half of Ensign Group. On maintenance cash generation - operating cash flow less depreciation-level spending, less the joint-venture partners' distributions - it produces about $6.74 a share, a 5.9% yield. So the four house valuation models reading deeply negative margins of safety are all making the same error, which is to treat expansion spending as if it were required to stand still.

Net: the market is roughly right on this name, which is an unusual and uncomfortable conclusion, and it is the honest one. Both the bullish street targets and the bearish cash-flow screens are wrong for opposite reasons that largely cancel. Fair value is close to today's price.

# Encompass Health (EHC) - Forensic Dossier

**Prepared:** 2026-07-27 · **Price used:** $115.105 (NYSE, US dollars, live quote) · **Transcripts reviewed:** Q1 2025 through Q1 2026 (five consecutive quarterly calls)

Encompass Health is the largest owner and operator of inpatient rehabilitation hospitals in the United States - roughly 169 hospitals that take patients straight from acute-care hospitals after a stroke, brain injury, major trauma or complex medical event, and rehabilitate them intensively before sending them home. About 97% of revenue comes from that single inpatient business; a small and deliberately shrinking outpatient therapy operation makes up the rest.

---

## 1. Narrative arc

The story management tells has been remarkably stable across all five calls, which is itself a finding. There is no pivot here, no quietly dropped growth driver, and no new vocabulary introduced to paper over a miss. What has changed is the *balance* of the story - and the shift is meaningful.

**Where it started (Q1 2025).** The pitch was pure capacity growth. Mark Tarr opened with 6.3% total discharge growth, 4.4% same-store, and spent his remarks on new hospitals: a joint-venture opening in Athens, Georgia, six more openings planned, a pipeline of ten hospitals with 500 beds beyond 2025. Regulation appeared once, briefly, as a favorable item - the proposed 2026 Medicare rate update of 2.6%. The framing was simply: demand exceeds supply, we are adding supply, watch the beds.

**The middle (Q2 and Q3 2025).** The demographic argument was formalized into a set-piece that now appears in every call: by 2030 one in five Americans will be 65 or older, the 75-plus population is growing about 4% a year, and the supply of licensed inpatient rehabilitation beds "has increased only nominally." Simultaneously, the capacity plan was raised three consecutive times - bed additions to existing hospitals for 2026 and 2027 went from roughly 120, to 120, to 150-200. Two new things entered the story here. First, an outside challenge: a July 2025 press investigation into care quality, which Tarr addressed defensively, noting the article covered "0.001% of our total discharges." Second, self-help - a large Oracle Fusion enterprise-software conversion and an expanding partnership with Palantir aimed at claims denials and admissions documentation.

**Where it is now (Q4 2025 and Q1 2026).** Regulation has moved from a footnote to a headline. Tarr's Q4 2025 remarks contain an explicit acknowledgment of "market anxiety regarding industry regulatory changes" and devote several paragraphs to two specific programs: the Review Choice Demonstration, a pre-payment claim-review regime that expanded into Texas on March 1 and California on May 1 of this year, and the Transforming Episode Accountability Model, a bundled-payment pilot that began January 1, 2026 and gives acute-care hospitals a financial incentive to route patients to cheaper settings. A third growth format was introduced - "small-format" satellite hospitals enabling a hub-and-spoke strategy, first one due 2027. And for the first time in five calls, management pre-committed to bad news: "This is not to say that we will be immune from short-term transitory impacts to our business" (Q1 2026).

**Net read:** the growth story has broadened (three expansion formats now, not two) while the risk disclosure has deepened. Nothing was dropped. Nothing was inflated. The arc is one of a management team that widened the aperture on its own risks at exactly the moment those risks became live.

---

## 2. Claims versus financials (forensic)

The test here is simple: management's words are the hypothesis, the numbers are the evidence.

| Management claim | Quarter | What the financials show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| "Premium labor spend in 2025 declined by more than $21 million from 2024, even as we added capacity" | Q4 2025 | Traceable quarter by quarter in the transcripts themselves: down $5.0M (Q1), $4.9M (Q2), $5.6M (Q3), $5.8M (Q4). Three themes recur, and management's handling differs sharply across them.

🔴 **Quality allegations remain unrebutted on their own terms** (Q2 2025 through today). ## 7. Hidden signals

**The vocabulary shift is from "adding beds" to "consolidating markets."** Across the five calls the company has closed a skilled-nursing unit in Lexington, two satellite locations in Cincinnati and Sewickley, a hosted unit in Bridgeport, West Virginia, and announced a 2027 closure in Evansville, Indiana. In each case the pattern is identical: exit a low-margin unit hosted inside somebody else's acute-care hospital, and rebuild the capacity as owned freestanding beds nearby. They then went further in Bridgeport - announcing on May 29, 2026 a new 36-bed freestanding hospital to replace the closed hosted unit. This is a deliberate migration from leased, partner-controlled beds toward owned real estate the company controls. It costs reported volume growth today and buys durability and margin later. It is also, quietly, why the same-store number looks worse than the business does.

**"Small-format hospitals" is the most consequential new phrase in the file** (introduced Q4 2025, elaborated Q1 2026). These operate under the same Medicare provider number as an existing hospital and share administrative services - meaning they extend the network into markets too small for a full hospital, without a new licence. That is a route around the very supply constraint that protects the incumbent position.

**A new voice arrived and speaks differently.** Pat Tuer was promoted to Chief Operating Officer in April 2025. Where Tarr and Coltharp defend, Tuer concedes: the higher acuity of managed-care patients is "great from a revenue perspective. But what that signals to me is there's a lot of other patients that should be coming to us that just aren't." On the outpatient business he was blunter than the prepared remarks - "I wouldn't read too much into the outpatient volume... it's really not a core business of ours." That is an operator talking, not an investor-relations voice, and it raises the information content of the calls.

**Capital allocation language has tilted toward buybacks.** Coltharp in Q1 2025: falling leverage "is creating capacity for us to allocate more capital to share repurchases... you should anticipate continued activity." The 2025 outcome confirmed it. This matters because it is the mechanism by which a growth-capital-heavy company still returns cash.

**A small, policy-exposed profit stream has quietly grown.** State Medicaid provider-tax programs contributed essentially nothing three or four years ago and about $21M of profit in 2026. Management guides it flat. It is small, but it is exactly the category of regulatory rent that current federal policy debate is aimed at.

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict (for the director)

**Trajectory: STRENGTHENING.** Every internal measure the company controls is moving the right way - margins, returns on capital, leverage, staff turnover, premium labor, cash generation across the full year, and the credibility of the guidance itself. The deterioration is confined to one line, same-store discharge growth, and a meaningful part of that is self-inflicted by deliberate market consolidation.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing:** *whether the Q1 2026 same-store deceleration to 1.6% is the closure artifact management says it is, or the beginning of a slower growth algorithm.* Everything in the valuation rests on the answer. The company's growth formula has been roughly 6-8% total discharge growth split between new capacity and same-store; if the same-store leg has permanently halved, the whole algorithm resets lower - and the stock is not priced for that. The second quarter report on August 5, 2026 is the first clean read, and it is also the first period carrying pre-payment claim review in Texas for a full quarter and California for most of one.

**Economic moat: NARROW, and WIDENING.**

The moat type is a *regulatory licence* reinforced by *scale-and-density*. Competitors cannot simply build an inpatient rehabilitation hospital: many states require a certificate-of-need approval, and federal rules require that a qualifying share of patients carry specific qualifying conditions, which caps who can operate in the category at all. The result, in management's words, is that licensed bed supply "has increased only nominally" while the 75-plus population grows about 4% a year. On top of that sits real density: 169 hospitals, an electronic medical record built specifically for this setting, protocols refined across more of these patients than any competitor treats, and - the most underrated asset - 67 hospitals operated as joint ventures with the acute-care hospitals that generate over 90% of referrals. A referral partner who co-owns the rehabilitation hospital is not a switchable customer.

The evidence says this moat is currently *widening*, not eroding: return on invested capital is rising (about 13.3% trailing against a mid-single-digit cost of capital), margins are expanding, occupancy is up more than 200 basis points, and the labor cost base is falling in absolute dollars while volumes grow. That is the opposite of the high-but-falling returns pattern that marks an eroding franchise.

Why narrow rather than wide: the price is not the company's to set. A single payer - Medicare, in fee-for-service and managed-care form - dominates the revenue base, and the annual rate is administered by a federal agency. A franchise whose pricing power is delegated to a regulator is real and defensible, but it is not the same thing as owning the price.

**Secular threat: MATERIAL, not terminal - reimbursement compression.**

The structural force to fear is not technology; it is policy. Four vectors are live simultaneously: the pre-payment claim-review programme now running in Texas and California; the bundled-payment pilot that pays acute-care hospitals to route patients to cheaper settings; managed-care pre-authorization friction, which management describes as "still a grind every day"; and periodic policy interest in paying the same rate regardless of care setting, which would strike directly at the rate premium this business earns. Add roughly $21M of state provider-tax profit sitting in the same policy crosshairs.

But three things argue against calling this terminal. The demographic arithmetic is genuinely large and genuinely slow - management's own framing, that roughly 35 million Medicare beneficiaries will remain outside managed care by 2030 against the company's 266,000 annual discharges, is not marketing. The supply of competing beds is structurally fixed. And the historical base rate favors the incumbent: bundled-payment pilots of one form or another have run continuously since 2014, and the company has posted positive discharge growth every year except 2020.

**Is the setup a fear-print or a shrinking base?** Neither, which is the honest answer. This is not a mispriced fear-print: the whole hospital sector has been savaged this year on reimbursement anxiety - the large acute-care operators trade roughly 30-39% below their own 52-week highs - and Encompass Health has conspicuously *not* participated in that de-rating, sitting about 10% off its high and above its 200-day average. The market has already sorted this company out of the distressed cohort. Nor is it a value trap: the earnings base is growing, not melting, and returns are rising. What it is, is a good business trading at a fair price with a live regulatory question and a decelerating volume line. Size for quality, not for discount.

interrogator_dossier:
# Encompass Health (EHC) - Forensic Dossier

**Prepared:** 2026-07-27 · **Price used:** $115.105 (NYSE, US dollars, live quote) · **Transcripts reviewed:** Q1 2025 through Q1 2026 (five consecutive quarterly calls)

Encompass Health is the largest owner and operator of inpatient rehabilitation hospitals in the United States - roughly 169 hospitals that take patients straight from acute-care hospitals after a stroke, brain injury, major trauma or complex medical event, and rehabilitate them intensively before sending them home. About 97% of revenue comes from that single inpatient business; a small and deliberately shrinking outpatient therapy operation makes up the rest.

---

## 1. Narrative arc

The story management tells has been remarkably stable across all five calls, which is itself a finding. There is no pivot here, no quietly dropped growth driver, and no new vocabulary introduced to paper over a miss. What has changed is the *balance* of the story - and the shift is meaningful.

**Where it started (Q1 2025).** The pitch was pure capacity growth. Mark Tarr opened with 6.3% total discharge growth, 4.4% same-store, and spent his remarks on new hospitals: a joint-venture opening in Athens, Georgia, six more openings planned, a pipeline of ten hospitals with 500 beds beyond 2025. Regulation appeared once, briefly, as a favorable item - the proposed 2026 Medicare rate update of 2.6%. The framing was simply: demand exceeds supply, we are adding supply, watch the beds.

**The middle (Q2 and Q3 2025).** The demographic argument was formalized into a set-piece that now appears in every call: by 2030 one in five Americans will be 65 or older, the 75-plus population is growing about 4% a year, and the supply of licensed inpatient rehabilitation beds "has increased only nominally." Simultaneously, the capacity plan was raised three consecutive times - bed additions to existing hospitals for 2026 and 2027 went from roughly 120, to 120, to 150-200. Two new things entered the story here. First, an outside challenge: a July 2025 press investigation into care quality, which Tarr addressed defensively, noting the article covered "0.001% of our total discharges." Second, self-help - a large Oracle Fusion enterprise-software conversion and an expanding partnership with Palantir aimed at claims denials and admissions documentation.

**Where it is now (Q4 2025 and Q1 2026).** Regulation has moved from a footnote to a headline. Tarr's Q4 2025 remarks contain an explicit acknowledgment of "market anxiety regarding industry regulatory changes" and devote several paragraphs to two specific programs: the Review Choice Demonstration, a pre-payment claim-review regime that expanded into Texas on March 1 and California on May 1 of this year, and the Transforming Episode Accountability Model, a bundled-payment pilot that began January 1, 2026 and gives acute-care hospitals a financial incentive to route patients to cheaper settings. A third growth format was introduced - "small-format" satellite hospitals enabling a hub-and-spoke strategy, first one due 2027. And for the first time in five calls, management pre-committed to bad news: "This is not to say that we will be immune from short-term transitory impacts to our business" (Q1 2026).

**Net read:** the growth story has broadened (three expansion formats now, not two) while the risk disclosure has deepened. Nothing was dropped. Nothing was inflated. The arc is one of a management team that widened the aperture on its own risks at exactly the moment those risks became live.

---

## 2. Claims versus financials (forensic)

The test here is simple: management's words are the hypothesis, the numbers are the evidence.

| Management claim | Quarter | What the financials show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| "Premium labor spend in 2025 declined by more than $21 million from 2024, even as we added capacity" | Q4 2025 | Traceable quarter by quarter in the transcripts themselves: down $5.0M (Q1), $4.9M (Q2), $5.6M (Q3), $5.8M (Q4). Sums to $21.3M. Contract labor fell to 1.1% of full-time staff, the lowest since Q1 2021 | Holds exactly |
| Operating leverage from higher occupancy | Q2 2025 onward | 2025 revenue grew 10.5% while adjusted operating profit grew 14.9%; 2026 first quarter revenue grew 9.0% against operating profit growth of 11.2%. Net margin 9.5% and expanding; return on invested capital about 13.3% on a trailing basis and rising | Holds, though the gap narrowed in Q1 2026 |
| Free cash flow strength funds everything internally | Every call | 2025 adjusted free cash flow $818M, up 18.5%, funding $736M of capital spending, $158M of buybacks and $71M of dividends with long-term debt essentially flat. Net leverage fell from 2.2x to 1.9x | Holds |
| Demand is "considerably underserved" and volume growth is durable | Every call | This is where the story is now **richer than the trajectory justifies.** Same-store discharge growth ran above 4% for twelve consecutive quarters through 2025 - and then printed **1.6% in Q1 2026**. Management attributes about 85 basis points to four deliberate unit closures, which still leaves roughly 2.5% underlying, little more than half the prior run rate | Diverges - the single most important gap in the file |
| Quality outcomes exceed industry averages | Every call | The company's own reported metrics are consistent and improving (discharge-to-community 84.5%, discharge-to-skilled-nursing down to 6.2% in Q1 2026). But federal readmission data cited by a July 2025 press investigation reached the opposite conclusion for 34 named facilities, and that dispute is now the basis of shareholder legal investigations | Unresolved, and management has not engaged the specific data |
| Capital returns are rising | Q1 2025 onward | Verified and continuing: the quarterly dividend went $0.17, then $0.19, then $0.21 (declared July 23, 2026, payable October 15). Buybacks in Q1 2025 alone exceeded all of 2024 | Holds |

Two numbers the narrative does not mention, which the director should weigh. First, **free cash flow turned down**: Q1 2026 adjusted free cash flow was $193.8M, a 12.9% decline year over year, even as profits grew - the growth-capital program is now consuming cash faster than earnings are adding it. Second, the **cost of debt stepped up**: on May 14, 2026 the company priced $500M of 5.875% notes due 2034 and simultaneously called $400M of 4.500% notes due 2028. That is roughly 140 basis points more expensive on that tranche, in a market our own regime work reads as roughly two-in-three likely to see another Federal Reserve hike by December. No maturity wall - but the cost of funding a program that consumes about 12% of revenue in capital spending is moving the wrong way.

---

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

**Rating: Stable, with confidence quietly rebalancing from offense toward preparation.**

- **Q1 2025 - offensive.** "We are pleased to report another strong quarter." Guidance raised. Capital plans raised. The only defensive note is a benefits-expense line growing 14% per employee, and it is explained away as a comparison artifact off a 0.7% base.
- **Q2 2025 - offensive, with the first external bruise.** Revenue up 12%, profit up 17.2%, guidance raised again. But Tarr's answer about the press investigation is the first genuinely defensive passage in the file: he calls the coverage "a mischaracterization" and leans on the sample size rather than the substance.
- **Q3 2025 - measured.** Growth decelerated to 9.4% revenue and 11.4% profit, and Doug Coltharp opens with pre-emptive framing: "quarterly fluctuations in discharge volume growth... is a normal expectation of our business model." That sentence is the tell. Free cash flow fell 8.2% in the quarter on working capital. He discloses the enterprise-software conversion costs and a property-tax charge without being asked.
- **Q4 2025 - confident, but the risk section is now load-bearing.** Tarr calls 2025 "stellar" and says "our company has never before been presented with greater opportunity." In the same remarks he devotes several paragraphs to regulatory anxiety and reaches for the historical analogy - prior bundled-payment pilots where "concerns regarding the impact to our patient flows were greatly overstated."
- **Q1 2026 - guarded confidence.** Guidance raised for the fifth consecutive quarter. Turnover among nurses hit 17.8%, the lowest since at least 2012. And then the explicit hedge: "we will not be immune from short-term transitory impacts."

Guidance has become *more* specific over time, not less - the hallmark of a team that is not managing a problem. But the centre of gravity of the prepared remarks has migrated from beds to rules.

---

## 4. Guidance credibility

**Reliability: High.**

The record across the five calls is a straight line of raises, each attributed to the quarter that had just closed rather than to a hoped-for second half:

| Call | Full-year revenue guide | Full-year adjusted profit guide | Adjusted earnings per share |
|---|---|---|---|
| Q1 2025 | $5.85 - 5.925B | $1.185 - 1.220B | $4.85 - 5.10 |
| Q2 2025 | $5.88 - 5.98B | $1.22 - 1.25B | $5.12 - 5.34 |
| Q3 2025 | raised again | raised again | raised again |
| Delivered 2025 | ~$5.94B | ~$1.258B | $5.54 |
| Q4 2025 (initial 2026) | $6.365 - 6.465B | $1.34 - 1.38B | $5.81 - 6.10 |
| Q1 2026 (raised) | $6.375 - 6.470B | $1.35 - 1.38B | $5.89 - 6.11 |

Delivered results landed at or above the top of the ranges set two and three quarters earlier, and the screener records a 100% earnings-beat rate across the last seven quarters. Free cash flow guidance was raised three separate times during 2025 ($620-715M, then $705-795M, then $730-810M) and the year finished at $818M - above the top of the final range.

**Is this sandbagging?** Partly, and honestly so. Coltharp repeatedly declines to extrapolate favorable one-offs - on the unusually strong first-quarter 2025 pricing he said plainly, "we don't believe that one quarter makes a trend. So we're not assuming that this flip... will sustain itself." That is conservative guidance-setting, not deception, and it is the reason the beat rate is 100%. The director should discount the beat rate accordingly: it measures guidance conservatism as much as operating outperformance.

---

## 5. Analyst pressure points

Three themes recur, and management's handling differs sharply across them.

**Answered well - Medicare Advantage friction.** Asked repeatedly (John Ransom Q1 2025, Jared Haase Q3 2025, Raj Kumar Q1 2026) whether managed-care plans are squeezing them, management gives specific, checkable answers: the ratio of admissions to referrals for Medicare Advantage is "substantially below" fee-for-service; the reimbursement gap between the two narrowed to 1% in Q1 2026 as acuity rose; a new admit-and-appeal strategy started mid-February 2026 produced a first favorable overturn. Pat Tuer volunteered the uncomfortable interpretation himself: higher Medicare Advantage acuity "signals to me is there's a lot of other patients that should be coming to us that just aren't."

**Answered incompletely - the quality allegations.** Brian Tanquilut (Q2 2025) and Raj Kumar (Q3 2025) both asked about the press investigation. Both times management answered about *referral patterns* - "we've not seen any negative fallout" - rather than about the underlying federal readmission data. That data is precisely what the shareholder investigations announced in March and April 2026 are built on. This is the one place in five calls where the company redirected rather than engaged.

**Asked but not yet resolved - the shape of volume growth.** Raj Kumar pressed in Q2 2025 on whether twelve straight quarters above 4% had "raised the bar in terms of the comp," and Coltharp agreed it had. Three quarters later the answer arrived: 1.6%. Analysts identified the risk before management quantified it, which is the pattern worth watching.

**Not being asked, and it should be:** nobody has pressed on why free cash flow fell 12.9% in Q1 2026, nor on the return profile of the accelerating bed program. Management raised the capital plan four separate times across these calls. On the software conversion Coltharp said openly, "it's not something that was done for a specific return on investment, and therefore, we're not looking to quantify a specific impact." That candour is admirable, but the same absence of a stated return hurdle now spans a much larger spending program.

---

## 6. Red flags and green flags

🔴 **Same-store discharge growth collapsed from a twelve-quarter run above 4% to 1.6% in Q1 2026.** Even crediting management's 85-basis-point closure adjustment, the underlying rate roughly halved. This is the load-bearing number in the whole file.

🔴 **Quality allegations remain unrebutted on their own terms** (Q2 2025 through today). Federal readmission data covering 34 named facilities is the basis of shareholder legal investigations opened in March and April 2026, and management's public answers have addressed referral volumes rather than the readmission statistics.

🔴 **Free cash flow turned negative year over year in Q1 2026** (down 12.9% to $193.8M) while profits grew - the capital program is now consuming the incremental earnings.

🔴 **Cost of debt stepped up about 140 basis points** on the tranche refinanced in May 2026, into a rate regime that is more likely to tighten than ease.

🔴 **Insiders sold and did not buy** - zero open-market purchases against twelve sales totalling 193,117 shares. Not fatal on its own, but it is the opposite of a conviction signal at a price near the highs.

🟢 **Labor - the industry's hardest problem - is being solved, visibly and repeatedly.** Nurse turnover fell from 20.4% to 17.8%, the lowest since at least 2012; therapist turnover from 7.7% to 6.4%; premium labor down five consecutive quarters and down $21M across 2025.

🟢 **Guidance raised in five consecutive quarters**, each time attributed to a quarter already banked rather than to a hoped-for recovery.

🟢 **The balance sheet strengthened while the company grew**: net leverage 2.2x to 1.9x, roughly $950M undrawn on the revolving facility, long-term debt essentially flat through a year of $736M capital spending.

🟢 **Management volunteers bad news with specificity** - the 85-basis-point closure drag, the 70-basis-point 2026 headwind from the West Virginia unit closure with 35-40 basis points expected to be recovered, the write-off of 2013-vintage claims in Q1 2026, the software-conversion cost overrun. None of these were dragged out by analysts.

🟢 **A major systems conversion landed cleanly** (Oracle Fusion, October 3, 2025) - "we threw the switch on October 3 and the lights didn't go out."

---

## 7. Hidden signals

**The vocabulary shift is from "adding beds" to "consolidating markets."** Across the five calls the company has closed a skilled-nursing unit in Lexington, two satellite locations in Cincinnati and Sewickley, a hosted unit in Bridgeport, West Virginia, and announced a 2027 closure in Evansville, Indiana. In each case the pattern is identical: exit a low-margin unit hosted inside somebody else's acute-care hospital, and rebuild the capacity as owned freestanding beds nearby. They then went further in Bridgeport - announcing on May 29, 2026 a new 36-bed freestanding hospital to replace the closed hosted unit. This is a deliberate migration from leased, partner-controlled beds toward owned real estate the company controls. It costs reported volume growth today and buys durability and margin later. It is also, quietly, why the same-store number looks worse than the business does.

**"Small-format hospitals" is the most consequential new phrase in the file** (introduced Q4 2025, elaborated Q1 2026). These operate under the same Medicare provider number as an existing hospital and share administrative services - meaning they extend the network into markets too small for a full hospital, without a new licence. That is a route around the very supply constraint that protects the incumbent position.

**A new voice arrived and speaks differently.** Pat Tuer was promoted to Chief Operating Officer in April 2025. Where Tarr and Coltharp defend, Tuer concedes: the higher acuity of managed-care patients is "great from a revenue perspective. But what that signals to me is there's a lot of other patients that should be coming to us that just aren't." On the outpatient business he was blunter than the prepared remarks - "I wouldn't read too much into the outpatient volume... it's really not a core business of ours." That is an operator talking, not an investor-relations voice, and it raises the information content of the calls.

**Capital allocation language has tilted toward buybacks.** Coltharp in Q1 2025: falling leverage "is creating capacity for us to allocate more capital to share repurchases... you should anticipate continued activity." The 2025 outcome confirmed it. This matters because it is the mechanism by which a growth-capital-heavy company still returns cash.

**A small, policy-exposed profit stream has quietly grown.** State Medicaid provider-tax programs contributed essentially nothing three or four years ago and about $21M of profit in 2026. Management guides it flat. It is small, but it is exactly the category of regulatory rent that current federal policy debate is aimed at.

---

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict (for the director)

**Trajectory: STRENGTHENING.** Every internal measure the company controls is moving the right way - margins, returns on capital, leverage, staff turnover, premium labor, cash generation across the full year, and the credibility of the guidance itself. The deterioration is confined to one line, same-store discharge growth, and a meaningful part of that is self-inflicted by deliberate market consolidation.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing:** *whether the Q1 2026 same-store deceleration to 1.6% is the closure artifact management says it is, or the beginning of a slower growth algorithm.* Everything in the valuation rests on the answer. The company's growth formula has been roughly 6-8% total discharge growth split between new capacity and same-store; if the same-store leg has permanently halved, the whole algorithm resets lower - and the stock is not priced for that. The second quarter report on August 5, 2026 is the first clean read, and it is also the first period carrying pre-payment claim review in Texas for a full quarter and California for most of one.

The moat type is a *regulatory licence* reinforced by *scale-and-density*. # Encompass Health (EHC) — Forensic Dossier

*Prepared for the investment committee. Source material: eight consecutive quarterly
earnings calls (Q1 2025 through Q1 2026) plus the screener's financial trajectory. All
quotes carry their quarter reference. Live price used: $111.07 (New York Stock Exchange),
as of 2026-08-02.*

Encompass Health is the largest operator of inpatient rehabilitation hospitals in the
United States — the facilities that take patients after a stroke, major trauma, or brain
injury and get them back to independence. It runs 169-plus hospitals, roughly 40% of them
joint ventures with local acute-care hospital systems.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story has been remarkably steady across all eight quarters, which is itself the
headline. From Q1 2025 to Q1 2026 management told one coherent tale: demand for inpatient
rehabilitation is structurally under-served, the supply of licensed beds barely grows, the
population aged 75-plus grows about 4% a year, and Encompass is pouring cash into new
hospitals and added beds to fill that gap. Every quarter opened with double-digit revenue
growth, mid-teens adjusted operating-earnings growth, and a guidance raise — a metronome.

What *expanded* over the year was the capacity ambition and the toolkit. The announced
new-hospital pipeline grew from "10 hospitals with 500 beds" (Q1 2025) to "14 hospitals
with 690 beds" (Q3 2025), then to a running pipeline described as "more than 40 projects."
Bed-addition targets for 2026 and 2027 were repeatedly lifted (from ~120 a year to
150–200). A genuinely new growth lever appeared: the "small-format hospital," a hub-and-spoke
satellite launching in 2027 (introduced Q4 2025, reaffirmed Q1 2026). The Palantir
data partnership was quietly widened from claims-denial work toward market analysis and
clinical staffing (Q4 2025, Q1 2026).

What was *added defensively* was regulatory preparation. Later calls (Q4 2025, Q1 2026)
devoted real airtime to three reimbursement changes — Review Choice Demonstration (a
pre-payment claims-audit regime) expanding into Texas and California, the TEAM model (a
Medicare episodic-payment pilot) starting January 2026, and Medicare Advantage
pre-authorization friction. Nothing was dropped or walked back; the demand thesis stayed
intact throughout.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | The financial evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Another strong quarter… raising guidance" (every call) | Revenue 2021→2025: $4.01B → $5.94B; net income $412M → $566M; EPS $4.11 → $5.54. 2025 revenue +10.5%, adjusted operating earnings +14.9%. Beat 7 of 7 quarters. | Matches — richer, if anything |
| Volume is broad-based and durable | 12 straight quarters of same-store discharge growth above 4% (cited Q2 2025); total discharges +6.3% (Q1'25), +7.2% (Q2'25), +5% (Q3'25), +5.3% (Q4'25), +4.3% (Q1'26) | Matches, decelerating as comps toughen |
| Labor pressure is easing | Premium labor spend fell >$21M in 2025; RN turnover hit 17.8% in Q1 2026, "lowest since at least 2012"; contract labor ~1.1–1.3% of staff | Matches — a real, quantified win |
| Cash generation is strong | 2025 adjusted free cash flow $818M, +18.5%. BUT the screener's trailing-twelve-month free cash flow reads just $464M and price-to-free-cash-flow 25.8x | Diverges by definition — see note |
| Balance sheet is conservative | Net leverage fell to 1.9x by year-end 2025; net debt ~$2.59B including leases | Matches |
| Returns are attractive | Return on equity 21.8%, return on invested capital 13.5%, gross margin ~96% and expanding | Matches — top of the peer group |

The one number that deserves a flag is free cash flow. Management's "$818M adjusted free
cash flow" and the screener's "$464M trailing free cash flow" are both true — they measure
different things. The company is spending heavily on *growth* capital: $736M of capital
expenditure in 2025, most of it new hospitals rather than maintenance. Conventional free
cash flow (operating cash minus *all* capital spending) is therefore modest and the
25.8x multiple looks expensive; the company's adjusted figure strips out the growth spend
to show the underlying engine. The honest read: this is a compounder reinvesting almost
everything it earns, so it should be valued on earnings power and returns on that
reinvestment, not on a bare free-cash-flow yield.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rising and, by year-end, almost serene.** Q1 2025: "We are pleased to report another
strong quarter." Q4 2025: "capping a stellar 2025… our focus is on the future, which for
Encompass Health is very bright… our company has never before been presented with greater
opportunity." Q1 2026: "We are pleased with our start to 2026." Confidence has been
consistently offensive — growth, capacity, market share — not defensive. Even the pivot to
discussing regulation reads as pre-emptive reassurance rather than alarm: "Regulatory change
is a constant in our business, and we have a long track record of successfully adapting"
(Q4 2025). Guidance specificity increased over the year (they now hand out precise revenue,
operating-earnings, and per-share ranges each quarter). No hedging creep, no new qualifiers.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY — **High.**

This is the strongest single fact in the file. Management raised full-year guidance in
*every* quarter of 2025, then delivered at or above the top of the raised range: 2025
adjusted per-share earnings finished at $5.54 (screener) against an initial 2025 range that
started at $4.85–$5.10 (Q1 2025) — they beat their own opening guide by roughly 10%. The
screener records a 7-of-7 quarterly earnings-beat rate. There is a mild but healthy
sandbagging pattern: initial ranges look conservative and get walked up. 2026 guidance was
set at $5.81–$6.10 per share (Q4 2025) and already raised once after Q1 2026. Reliability
is High, with the only caveat that a 100% beat rate sets a bar that eventually breaks — the
first in-line quarter will feel like a miss to a market trained to expect raises.

Analysts circled three worries all year, and management met each with data rather than
deflection:
- **Medicare Advantage friction** (John Ransom Q1'25, Jared Haase Q3'25, Brian Tanquilut
  Q4'25). Management conceded the "grind every day dealing with those plans" (Q3'25) on
  pre-authorization, but argued the friction actually pushes patients toward higher-paying
  fee-for-service as insurers exit MA geographies (Q1'26). Not a dodge — a reframe backed by
  a shrinking MA-vs-fee-for-service reimbursement gap (down to 1% in Q1'26).

  "mischaracterization" covering "0.001% of our total discharges" and reported "no negative
  fallout" in referral patterns two quarters running (Q2'25, Q3'25). Watchable but so far
  immaterial.
- **Regulatory change (RCD, TEAM)** — the most legitimate pressure point. Management's answer
  is a 93% claims-affirmation rate in its Alabama pilot and a long history of navigating
  prior payment models (Q4'25). Credible, not yet proven in Texas/California.

No topic that analysts pushed on later turned into disclosed bad news within the window.

cost tailwind, not a one-off.

quarter, with faster-than-expected Medicare certifications (Q4'25) — the growth engine
is high-return.
🟢 Leverage falling to 1.9x while self-funding all expansion, buybacks ($158M in 2025) and a
rising dividend — genuine financial flexibility.
🟢 The reimbursement gap between Medicare Advantage and fee-for-service compressed to ~1%
(Q1'26), removing a long-standing mix worry.
🔴 Free cash flow is thin on a conventional basis because growth capital spending is large;
if the high-return reinvestment runway ever shortens, the valuation loses its justification.

a merely-in-line quarter — the setup is priced for continuation.
🔴 Insider behavior is one-sided: zero open-market purchases against twelve open-market sales
(193,117 shares) — no conviction buying, though nothing unusual for a steady compounder.
🟡 Reimbursement changes (RCD in Texas/California from March 2026, TEAM from January 2026) are
real and still early — "not… immune from short-term transitory impacts" (Q1'26).

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- **Vocabulary shift toward technology and efficiency.** The Palantir relationship moved from
  a footnote to a named lever across claims denials, market analysis, and clinical staffing
  (Q4'25, Q1'26), and the October 2025 Oracle Fusion enterprise-software conversion went live
  "without significant disruptions." Management explicitly declined to attach a dollar
  return to it — honest, but it means the efficiency upside is optionality, not guidance.
- **Capital allocation tilting toward buybacks.** Q1'25 repurchases alone "slightly exceeded
  those… for all of 2024," and management signaled "continued activity." With leverage low
  and expansion self-funded, the surplus is increasingly returned — a quiet supportive bid.
- **A new growth format.** The small-format hub-and-spoke hospital (2027) is the first
  genuinely new expansion modality in years and hints the core de-novo runway, while long, is
  being supplemented deliberately.
- **Chief Operating Officer role created** (Pat Tuer promoted, Q1'25) — an
  organizational build-out consistent with, not ahead of, the growth.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: STRENGTHENING.** This is a high-quality, well-run compounder executing a clear,
demographically-tailwinded plan with credible, repeatedly-beaten guidance and an improving
cost and balance-sheet profile.

business is excellent and the numbers are clean; the question is entirely whether $111 —
roughly 18–19x this year's expected earnings and about 10x enterprise value to operating
earnings — leaves enough margin of safety. On conservative models it does not. The forensic
work argues for patience at a better entry, not for doubting the franchise.

entrant cannot easily replicate. The width shows in the evidence: return on invested capital
~13.5% and rising, gross margin ~96% and expanding, and market-share gains against skilled
nursing facilities. That is a widening moat, not an eroding one.

reimbursement compression — the risk that Medicare and Medicare Advantage squeeze rates or
tighten admission criteria (RCD, TEAM). It is a genuine, permanent headwind on the
sector, but the demand side (an aging population, a widening bed-supply gap) is growing
faster than the rate pressure, and management has navigated every prior version of these
models while still growing. The cheapness question here is about a fair price for a good
compounder, not a structurally shrinking base — this is not a value trap, but neither is it
a fear-print bargain.

# Encompass Health (EHC) — Forensic Dossier

*Prepared for the investment committee. Source material: eight consecutive quarterly
earnings calls (Q1 2025 through Q1 2026) plus the screener's financial trajectory. All
quotes carry their quarter reference. Live price used: $111.07 (New York Stock Exchange),
as of 2026-08-02.*

Encompass Health is the largest operator of inpatient rehabilitation hospitals in the
United States — the facilities that take patients after a stroke, major trauma, or brain
injury and get them back to independence. It runs 169-plus hospitals, roughly 40% of them
joint ventures with local acute-care hospital systems.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story has been remarkably steady across all eight quarters, which is itself the
headline. From Q1 2025 to Q1 2026 management told one coherent tale: demand for inpatient
rehabilitation is structurally under-served, the supply of licensed beds barely grows, the
population aged 75-plus grows about 4% a year, and Encompass is pouring cash into new
hospitals and added beds to fill that gap. Every quarter opened with double-digit revenue
growth, mid-teens adjusted operating-earnings growth, and a guidance raise — a metronome.

What *expanded* over the year was the capacity ambition and the toolkit. The announced
new-hospital pipeline grew from "10 hospitals with 500 beds" (Q1 2025) to "14 hospitals
with 690 beds" (Q3 2025), then to a running pipeline described as "more than 40 projects."
Bed-addition targets for 2026 and 2027 were repeatedly lifted (from ~120 a year to
150–200). A genuinely new growth lever appeared: the "small-format hospital," a hub-and-spoke
satellite launching in 2027 (introduced Q4 2025, reaffirmed Q1 2026). The Palantir
data partnership was quietly widened from claims-denial work toward market analysis and
clinical staffing (Q4 2025, Q1 2026).

What was *added defensively* was regulatory preparation. Later calls (Q4 2025, Q1 2026)
devoted real airtime to three reimbursement changes — Review Choice Demonstration (a
pre-payment claims-audit regime) expanding into Texas and California, the TEAM model (a
Medicare episodic-payment pilot) starting January 2026, and Medicare Advantage
pre-authorization friction. Nothing was dropped or walked back; the demand thesis stayed
intact throughout.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | The financial evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Another strong quarter… raising guidance" (every call) | Revenue 2021→2025: $4.01B → $5.94B; net income $412M → $566M; EPS $4.11 → $5.54. 2025 revenue +10.5%, adjusted operating earnings +14.9%. Beat 7 of 7 quarters. | Matches — richer, if anything |
| Volume is broad-based and durable | 12 straight quarters of same-store discharge growth above 4% (cited Q2 2025); total discharges +6.3% (Q1'25), +7.2% (Q2'25), +5% (Q3'25), +5.3% (Q4'25), +4.3% (Q1'26) | Matches, decelerating as comps toughen |
| Labor pressure is easing | Premium labor spend fell >$21M in 2025; RN turnover hit 17.8% in Q1 2026, "lowest since at least 2012"; contract labor ~1.1–1.3% of staff | Matches — a real, quantified win |
| Cash generation is strong | 2025 adjusted free cash flow $818M, +18.5%. BUT the screener's trailing-twelve-month free cash flow reads just $464M and price-to-free-cash-flow 25.8x | Diverges by definition — see note |
| Balance sheet is conservative | Net leverage fell to 1.9x by year-end 2025; net debt ~$2.59B including leases | Matches |
| Returns are attractive | Return on equity 21.8%, return on invested capital 13.5%, gross margin ~96% and expanding | Matches — top of the peer group |

The one number that deserves a flag is free cash flow. Management's "$818M adjusted free
cash flow" and the screener's "$464M trailing free cash flow" are both true — they measure
different things. The company is spending heavily on *growth* capital: $736M of capital
expenditure in 2025, most of it new hospitals rather than maintenance. Conventional free
cash flow (operating cash minus *all* capital spending) is therefore modest and the
25.8x multiple looks expensive; the company's adjusted figure strips out the growth spend
to show the underlying engine. The honest read: this is a compounder reinvesting almost
everything it earns, so it should be valued on earnings power and returns on that
reinvestment, not on a bare free-cash-flow yield.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rising and, by year-end, almost serene.** Q1 2025: "We are pleased to report another
strong quarter." Q4 2025: "capping a stellar 2025… our focus is on the future, which for
Encompass Health is very bright… our company has never before been presented with greater
opportunity." Q1 2026: "We are pleased with our start to 2026." Confidence has been
consistently offensive — growth, capacity, market share — not defensive. Even the pivot to
discussing regulation reads as pre-emptive reassurance rather than alarm: "Regulatory change
is a constant in our business, and we have a long track record of successfully adapting"
(Q4 2025). Guidance specificity increased over the year (they now hand out precise revenue,
operating-earnings, and per-share ranges each quarter). No hedging creep, no new qualifiers.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY — **High.**

This is the strongest single fact in the file. Management raised full-year guidance in
*every* quarter of 2025, then delivered at or above the top of the raised range: 2025
adjusted per-share earnings finished at $5.54 (screener) against an initial 2025 range that
started at $4.85–$5.10 (Q1 2025) — they beat their own opening guide by roughly 10%. The
screener records a 7-of-7 quarterly earnings-beat rate. There is a mild but healthy
sandbagging pattern: initial ranges look conservative and get walked up. 2026 guidance was
set at $5.81–$6.10 per share (Q4 2025) and already raised once after Q1 2026. Reliability
is High, with the only caveat that a 100% beat rate sets a bar that eventually breaks — the
first in-line quarter will feel like a miss to a market trained to expect raises.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Analysts circled three worries all year, and management met each with data rather than
deflection:
- **Medicare Advantage friction** (John Ransom Q1'25, Jared Haase Q3'25, Brian Tanquilut
  Q4'25). Management conceded the "grind every day dealing with those plans" (Q3'25) on
  pre-authorization, but argued the friction actually pushes patients toward higher-paying
  fee-for-service as insurers exit MA geographies (Q1'26). Not a dodge — a reframe backed by
  a shrinking MA-vs-fee-for-service reimbursement gap (down to 1% in Q1'26).
- **A negative press article on quality** (surfaced Q2'25). Management called it a
  "mischaracterization" covering "0.001% of our total discharges" and reported "no negative
  fallout" in referral patterns two quarters running (Q2'25, Q3'25). Watchable but so far
  immaterial.
- **Regulatory change (RCD, TEAM)** — the most legitimate pressure point. Management's answer
  is a 93% claims-affirmation rate in its Alabama pilot and a long history of navigating
  prior payment models (Q4'25). Credible, not yet proven in Texas/California.

No topic that analysts pushed on later turned into disclosed bad news within the window.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🟢 Turnover at a multi-decade low and premium labor down >$21M (Q4'25, Q1'26) — a durable
cost tailwind, not a one-off.
🟢 Four of eight 2025-opened hospitals were already earnings-positive in their opening
quarter, with faster-than-expected Medicare certifications (Q4'25) — the growth engine
is high-return.
🟢 Leverage falling to 1.9x while self-funding all expansion, buybacks ($158M in 2025) and a
rising dividend — genuine financial flexibility.
🟢 The reimbursement gap between Medicare Advantage and fee-for-service compressed to ~1%
(Q1'26), removing a long-standing mix worry.
🔴 Free cash flow is thin on a conventional basis because growth capital spending is large;
if the high-return reinvestment runway ever shortens, the valuation loses its justification.
🔴 A 100% beat streak plus a stock in the middle of its 52-week range leaves little room for
a merely-in-line quarter — the setup is priced for continuation.
🔴 Insider behavior is one-sided: zero open-market purchases against twelve open-market sales
(193,117 shares) — no conviction buying, though nothing unusual for a steady compounder.
🟡 Reimbursement changes (RCD in Texas/California from March 2026, TEAM from January 2026) are
real and still early — "not… immune from short-term transitory impacts" (Q1'26).

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- **Vocabulary shift toward technology and efficiency.** The Palantir relationship moved from
  a footnote to a named lever across claims denials, market analysis, and clinical staffing
  (Q4'25, Q1'26), and the October 2025 Oracle Fusion enterprise-software conversion went live
  "without significant disruptions." Management explicitly declined to attach a dollar
  return to it — honest, but it means the efficiency upside is optionality, not guidance.
- **Capital allocation tilting toward buybacks.** Q1'25 repurchases alone "slightly exceeded
  those… for all of 2024," and management signaled "continued activity." With leverage low
  and expansion self-funded, the surplus is increasingly returned — a quiet supportive bid.
- **A new growth format.** The small-format hub-and-spoke hospital (2027) is the first
  genuinely new expansion modality in years and hints the core de-novo runway, while long, is
  being supplemented deliberately.
- **Chief Operating Officer role created** (Pat Tuer promoted, Q1'25) — an
  organizational build-out consistent with, not ahead of, the growth.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: STRENGTHENING.** This is a high-quality, well-run compounder executing a clear,
demographically-tailwinded plan with credible, repeatedly-beaten guidance and an improving
cost and balance-sheet profile.

The single most important thing to weigh before sizing is **price, not quality.** The
business is excellent and the numbers are clean; the question is entirely whether $111 —
roughly 18–19x this year's expected earnings and about 10x enterprise value to operating
earnings — leaves enough margin of safety. On conservative models it does not. The forensic
work argues for patience at a better entry, not for doubting the franchise.

**Economic moat: WIDE, and stable-to-widening.** The moat is a regulatory-license-plus-scale
moat. New inpatient-rehab capacity often requires a state Certificate of Need, a federal rule
limits which patients qualify for the setting, and Encompass's scale, clinical-outcome data,
and joint-venture ties to acute-care hospitals compound into referral advantages a new
entrant cannot easily replicate. The width shows in the evidence: return on invested capital
~13.5% and rising, gross margin ~96% and expanding, and market-share gains against skilled
nursing facilities. That is a widening moat, not an eroding one.

**Secular threat: manageable (not terminal).** The relevant structural force is
reimbursement compression — the risk that Medicare and Medicare Advantage squeeze rates or
tighten admission criteria (RCD, TEAM). It is a genuine, permanent headwind on the
sector, but the demand side (an aging population, a widening bed-supply gap) is growing
faster than the rate pressure, and management has navigated every prior version of these
models while still growing. The cheapness question here is about a fair price for a good
compounder, not a structurally shrinking base — this is not a value trap, but neither is it
a fear-print bargain.

CREDIBILITY_SCORE: 4 | TRAJECTORY: STRENGTHENING | MOAT: WIDE | MOAT_TREND: WIDENING | SECULAR_THREAT: manageable
